newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia economy accelerating strongly - forecaster.
newsitem.headline: Australia economy accelerating strongly - forecaster.

text.p: A leading Australian economics consultancy forecast on Monday a strong acceleration from the country's recent economic flat spot and an imminent return to four or five percent annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth.
If the Access Economics forecasts are achieved, Australia will have enjoyed its longest economic expansion phase since official quarterly growth estimates began in the late 1950s.
But Access said price pressure was rising again, especially in wages, and the Reserve Bank of Australia ought not to effect a fifth rate cut in the current series.

"Overall domestic demand troughed in September and is now rising fast -- with only stocks (business inventories) between it and a better bottom line for growth," Access said in its quarterly forecasting report.
The Australian economy grew 0.9 percent between the December and March quarters for an annual growth rate of 2.4 percent, the lowest since immediately after the recession of 1990 and 1991.

Recent falls in employment have reinforced the impression of a soft economy but Access argued that Australia had been reached the trough in economic growth at least nine months ago and had been growing at a rising rate since then.
Production, although acclerating, did not grow as fast as demand in the March quarter, and the gap was covered by a rundown in business inventories.
But inventories could run down forever and Access forecast production rising to the challenge of feeding demand.
Access saw GDP for the coming fiscal year, to June 1998, averaging a level 3.9 percent higher than in this year, a little stronger than the government forecast of 3.75 percent.
On that year-average basis, GDP growth would accelerate to 4.6 percent in 1998/99 before settling to 3.6 percent in the following year.
But the current fiscal year, let down by the stocks rundown, would show just 2.9 percent year-average growth, less than the government's forecast of 3.25 percent.
Australian inflation has been subdued lately, with policymakers' preferred "underlying" measure in the lower half of the Reserve Bank's two- to three-percent target range.
Access saw underlying inflation, which excludes irregular items, at a year-average 2.1 percent in 1996/97 and 1997/98 but jumping to 3.1 percent in the following two years.
The current price restraint had been delivered by modest wage growth, and the factors that had held down wages were about to reverse direction.
"Activity will rise while within overall growth the labour- and union-intensive sectors of the economy will lift," the consultancy said.
What little growth has appeared lately has been in capital-intensive sectors, depriving Australia of new jobs.
The trend unemployment rate, a figure that irons out the bumps in seasonally adjusted data, was 8.8 percent in May, up from an 8.4 percent trough recorded in the second half of 1995.
Access forecast economic growth continuing until at least mid-2005, which would amount to 14 years of unbroken expansion.
The previous post-1959 record was 8-1/2 years in the late 1960s and early 1970s.
